analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare home health coverage, paid for by raising the payroll tax cap on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill never left its House subcommittees and expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare only pays for home nursing and aide visits if they are 'intermittent,' a definition that has kept some seriously ill seniors from getting coverage. This bill would have spelled out that daily care still counts as intermittent in many cases, letting more homebound beneficiaries qualify. To pay for it, the bill raised the wage ceiling for the Medicare payroll tax, so higher-earning workers would contribute more. It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need daily — but not permanent — nursing or home health aide care at home. Under current law those services often fail the 'intermittent' test and are denied; the bill would have made such care coverable, reducing the choice between institutional care or unpaid family caregiving.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homebound Medicare beneficiaries needing daily care

how_it_helps.text: The bill redefines 'intermittent' home health services so that care needed less than 7 days a week qualifies, and care needed 7 days a week still qualifies for up to 40 consecutive days, making more home nursing and aide services eligible for Medicare coverage [S3].
It takes effect for home health periods beginning on or after January 1, 1993 [S3].

The expansion is financed by raising the cap on wages subject to the hospital insurance (Medicare) payroll tax: $5,000 above the 1992 base for 1993, then indexed to rise with the Social Security benefit base each year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers whose wages exceed the Medicare payroll tax cap. Raising the taxable wage base by $5,000 and indexing it upward means higher earners pay more in hospital insurance taxes, while most workers pay nothing extra.
analysis.who_pays_short: Higher-earning workers above the tax cap

drawbacks.text: The financing falls entirely on payroll taxes, which are paid by workers; raising the wage base increases the tax bill for employees and employers with above-cap wages, and employers share the increase [S2][S3].
The bill never specifies the fiscal size of the coverage expansion, so lawmakers had no stated estimate of how much tax increase the new home health benefit would require [S3].

Expanding Medicare home health coverage carries a well-known risk of rapid spending growth, since home health use historically expanded quickly whenever eligibility loosened — a cost an honest supporter would have had to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is a real one: a meaningful benefit for homebound seniors paid for by a modestly larger payroll tax on high earners, which is a progressive way to fund it. The bill's weakness is design, not intent — it specifies the tax increase mechanically but gives no estimate of the benefit's cost, and loosening the intermittent-care rule could have opened spending that was hard to cap. On balance it was a targeted, fiscally identified expansion that got no hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where nothing further happened before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Hoagland introduced the bill on May 21, 1992, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means [S1][S5].
On May 28 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and on June 5 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment [S5].
No markup, hearing, floor action, or vote followed, and the bill attracted no cosponsors [S4][S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died at that point [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare's finances were untouched, and employers and high-wage workers avoided the payroll tax increase. Homebound seniors who might have qualified for covered daily home care gained nothing, and the home health industry gained no new revenue stream.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-wage workers and employers; seniors gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Peter Hoagland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred jointly to the two committees with jurisdiction over Medicare.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with primary jurisdiction over Medicare financing
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health, where it sat with no markup or hearing before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicare coverage rules
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it sat with no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape is unknown; the only record is that it stalled in committee in a Democratic-controlled House.

industries.note: Broadening Medicare's intermittent-care rule would have made more patients eligible for covered home nursing and aide visits, sending new billable volume to home health providers. Their gain here comes from delivering care seniors and Medicare wanted, so it runs alongside the public's interest.
The bill raises the wage base for the hospital insurance tax, and employers pay a matching share of that payroll tax, so businesses with above-cap payrolls would have borne part of the cost.
